title: Still Operational
paragraphs: Andrew Walker had nearly finished tomorrow's patrol when Darius shouted, “Why does my soup pot have a serial number?”
Andrew kept his finger on the map.
From the kitchen came a scrape, a heavy clunk, and Juno's voice.
“That's on the bearing.”
“I can see that.”
“Then technically the pot doesn't.”
Andrew closed his eyes. He had one route left to check. One route, a note for the morning briefing, and then he could stop pretending the coffee beside his elbow was still worth drinking.
“Juno,” Darius said, much more quietly.
Andrew pushed back his chair.

His desk occupied the narrow office beside the hangar, close enough to the kitchen that he could usually tell what Darius was making. Tonight there had been onions frying, followed by the smell of bread. His stomach had been paying attention even when he hadn't.
He left the patrol map open and stepped into the corridor.

The kitchen door stood propped with a folded piece of cardboard. Beyond it, Darius held a steel pot in both hands. He was broad enough to make it look small, although Andrew knew from washing it that it could hold dinner for eight and become unpleasantly heavy afterward. A smear of flour crossed Darius's dark cheek. His apron was spotless except where he'd leaned against the worktop.

Juno stood on the other side of the table, blond hair sticking through the strap of his orange goggles. The high yellow collar of his jacket had folded beneath one ear. His headphones hung around his neck, one ear cup dangling by a wire.
Nico was beside him, trying to appear unconnected to either the pot or Juno. He had a spoon in his hand.
Andrew stopped in the doorway. “Am I early for dinner?”
Darius tilted the pot.
Something inside rolled against the steel with a thick, oily knock.
“Depends how you like your bearings,” Darius said.
Andrew looked inside. A metal ring the width of his palm lay in a shallow puddle of brown fluid. Black fingerprints marked the rim.
“Ah.”
“It's from the left front leg,” Juno said. “I couldn't leave it on the bench. Nico had everything laid out.”
“You told me to lay everything out,” Nico said.
“And you did. Beautifully. That's not the issue.”
“Put the spoon down,” Darius told him.
Nico looked at his hand as though he had discovered the spoon there.
“I was only seeing if the onions were done.”
“They are done. They have been done for twenty minutes. They are waiting for the rest of their dinner.”
Nico put the spoon on the table.
Andrew glanced at the clock above the sink. If they sorted this quickly, he could finish the map before everyone sat down.
“All right. Can we get the bearing out, clean the pot, and—”
“No,” Darius said.
The answer arrived fast enough to stop him.
Darius set the pot down carefully. “I'm not feeding anybody from that.”
Andrew looked again at the fluid. “Right. No. Bad suggestion.”
Juno rubbed a thumb over a black mark on his sleeve. “I was going to clean it before you needed it.”
“You said that yesterday.”
“Yesterday was a bowl.”
“Yes,” Darius said. “It was.”
Andrew pulled out the nearest chair and sat. The map could wait.
“Juno. Did you ask?”
Juno's eyes shifted toward Nico.
“Don't look at me,” Nico said. “I asked if you were sure.”
“That sounded supportive at the time.”
Darius folded his arms.
Juno's grin gave out. He looked at the chopped vegetables waiting in their bowls, then at the little patch of flour on Darius's cheek.
“No,” he said. “I didn't ask.”
The kitchen went quiet enough for Andrew to hear the oven fan rattle.
He knew that pause. Juno could spend half an hour explaining how something worked and struggle over six words about what he'd done.
Andrew waited.
“I'm sorry,” Juno said at last. “I thought I'd have it back before you noticed.”
“I would still have eaten out of it.”
“Yeah.” Juno swallowed. “I didn't think that far.”
Darius rubbed both hands over his face. “I just wanted to make a decent dinner.”

On the table stood a bowl of peeled potatoes, another of cabbage, two opened tins of beans and the onions Nico had been investigating. Someone had written STEW on the small board above the stove. Beneath it, in different handwriting, someone else had added WITH ACTUAL THINGS IN IT.
Andrew knew which part was Darius's.
“What can we do?” he asked.
Darius studied the ingredients. For a moment Andrew thought he might simply leave them there. Then he took a frying pan from the rack.
“Change dinner.”
“To what?” Nico asked.
“Something you can help with.”
Nico looked at Andrew.
Andrew spread his hands. “I've always believed in you.”
“Since when?”
“Just now. It's exciting.”
Juno let out a small laugh, then checked Darius's face before allowing himself another.
Darius pointed at the pot. “First, get that out of my kitchen. And wash your hands. Properly.”
Juno picked it up by both handles. “I'll replace it.”
“With a pot.”
“Yes.”
“A normal pot.”
Juno paused at the door.
Andrew shook his head at him.
“Normal pot,” Juno agreed.

Andrew followed him across the corridor to make sure the leaking rim stayed clear of the walls. The hangar doors were shut against the rain, and water ticked steadily into a bucket beneath one of the high windows. Their mechs stood along the bays with access panels open and service steps pulled up beside the cockpits.

Juno's XR-17 had its left front foot raised on a support. With the leg folded, Andrew could see the empty bearing housing and the fresh grease around its lip. Above it, the turret's cannon pointed down the bay between the upright missile pods. Someone had hung a pair of damp socks from the bottom of the cockpit ladder.
Andrew looked at Juno.
“They're Nico's.”
“I hadn't asked.”
“You were looking.”
Juno set the pot on the bench, clear of the parts Nico had arranged in earnest little rows. He caught Andrew studying the raised leg.
“New bearing's in the wrapping. Old one was starting to catch. It'll be ready tonight.”
Andrew crouched to look at the housing. “Tonight, or ready for tomorrow?”
“Tomorrow. I'll finish the install, cycle it, then do the check again when it's cold.”
“Put the results on the sheet. If it catches, tell me.”
Juno nodded. “I will.”
There was room on the bench for a second tray if they moved the empty packaging. Andrew started to reach for it, then stopped. Juno was already gathering it up.
“And I can do this after dinner,” Juno added.
“Good. Darius needs somebody to argue with his potatoes.”
Back in the kitchen, Nico had been given a knife and very little confidence. Darius stood beside him demonstrating how thin the potato slices needed to be.
“Like this.”
Nico held up his first attempt. It was thick enough to stand on its edge.
Darius considered it. “Smaller.”
“You said slices.”
“I did. You made a wheel.”
Andrew laughed. Nico pointed the knife at him.
“Away from people,” Darius said immediately.
Nico lowered it. “He hasn't got a job.”
Darius handed Andrew a cabbage.
“Tear that into pieces. Bowl's there.”
Andrew looked down at it. “How big?”
“Pieces. I'll tell you if they're wrong.”
It was a system Andrew understood. He rolled up his sleeves and got to work.

By the time Juno returned with damp hands and a cleaner expression, the kitchen had become difficult to move through. Darius managed them by pointing, occasionally taking a knife away, and saying “behind you” in a tone that made everybody shift at once.

Andrew tore the cabbage while Nico discovered that potatoes became slippery when held too tightly. Juno washed the bowls and tried to persuade Darius that the damaged headphones on his neck were an improvement because now he could hear people approaching.
“Then you should have heard me asking for my bowl yesterday,” Darius said.
“Working on the range.”
A camera clicked from the doorway.
Andrew looked up. Akari stood with one shoulder against the frame, her long black ponytail caught beneath the camera strap.
“No,” Andrew said.
She lowered the camera just enough to reveal her smile. “You don't know what I took.”
“I know you.”
“Darius, they're behaving. You need evidence.”
Darius glanced at the cabbage in Andrew's hands. “Take another. It might not happen again.”
Andrew held up a ragged leaf. “I was told there would be supervision.”
Akari untangled her hair from the strap, came inside and stole a crisp piece of potato from Darius's test batch. He tapped her knuckles with the handle of a wooden spoon, too late to save it.
“Hot,” she said, trying to smile around it.
“Yes,” Darius said.
Her eyes watered. Andrew slid a cup of water toward her. She took it without attempting another word.

The smell changed as the vegetables hit the pans. Butter, pepper and the sweet edges of the onions filled the little room. Andrew's stomach made a noise that Nico heard and would, unfortunately, remember.
Mara arrived carrying the patrol sheet.
“Found this on your desk,” she told Andrew.
His hands stopped over the bowl. “I was coming back.”

“I gathered.” Her long chestnut braid had slipped over one shoulder. She kept it out of the food while turning the sheet toward him. “The eastern crossing. We checked it this afternoon. Approach is washed out.”
Andrew leaned closer. He had drawn their withdrawal route straight through it.
“Passable?”
“Not if somebody needs towing.”
He pictured the bend, the soft shoulder, a disabled mech slowing the others. “We take the service road.”
Mara touched another line with her finger. “Longer, but there's room. And we can see anything coming across the fields.”
Andrew followed the line to the next junction. The Reclaimed had reached the road twice this week. He wanted space to turn if they reached it again.
“Agreed. Can you mark it?”
She took the pencil from behind her ear.
Darius moved a pan off the heat. “Can you mark it somewhere else?”
Andrew looked at the map hanging over the cabbage. “Sorry.”
Mara folded the sheet. “I'll leave it on your desk.”
“Thanks.”
She looked at him for a second, then at the leaf still in his hand.
“You're allowed to let go of that now.”
Andrew dropped it in the bowl.
Dinner was late, and there was no stew.

Darius brought out two pans of fried potatoes, cabbage and onions, with beans in a small saucepan and eight rolls wrapped in a clean cloth. The rolls had risen unevenly. He inspected the smallest one before putting it on his own plate.
Andrew exchanged it for his larger one while Darius went back for the spoon.

The common room had once belonged to people who liked wipe-clean furniture. They had inherited the furniture and improved it with cushions, taped photographs and a bookshelf made from packing crates. Rain blurred the high windows. An old projector occupied the shelf above a noticeboard crowded with repair requests and Nico's disputed tournament results.
Andrew took the seat nearest the door. He could still see his office across the corridor, the lamp bright over the unfinished work.
Yelena had already claimed the chair opposite Darius. Her long braid lay over the shoulder of a loose sweater, and she was shuffling a battered deck of cards.
“After dinner?” she asked him.
Darius set down the spoon. “You still owe me two biscuits.”
“A temporary delay in payment.”
“You ate them.”
“Which is causing the delay.”
Sera sat beside Akari with a paperback open against the water jug. She had gathered her curls into a loose bun, with a pencil through it that Andrew suspected she had been looking for all afternoon.
“Sera,” he said, touching the back of his own head.
She reached up, found the pencil and stared at it.
Akari hid her mouth behind her cup.
“You watched me look,” Sera told her.
“I thought you meant a different pencil.”
Sera put it inside her book and shut the cover with care.
Juno sat down last. He had scrubbed his nails, changed his jacket and carried in a stack of clean bowls nobody needed anymore.
For a moment he stood looking at the plates.
Darius took the bowls from him. “Tomorrow.”
“Right.”
“Sit down. It's getting cold.”
Juno sat.

Andrew waited until Darius had taken his first mouthful before trying his own. The potatoes were crisp at the edges and soft enough inside to come apart under his fork. He went back for more before he'd finished swallowing.
Darius watched him. “All right?”
“I'm deciding.”
“You've nearly finished it.”
“Thorough process.”
Nico pointed at his plate. “Some of those are mine.”
“We can tell,” Mara said, lifting a particularly substantial potato slice.
“That's the best one.”
Mara ate it. After chewing for a while, she nodded. “I'll let you know.”
Nico tried to take it well. Andrew gave him credit for almost managing.

Juno started explaining the bearing replacement with a fork in his hand. Darius listened long enough to ask whether the bad one was why the floor vibrated when Juno turned outside the hangar. Juno's whole face brightened. He abandoned his potatoes to demonstrate, using the salt tin and two rolls.
“Bread stays on the plates,” Darius said.
Juno put it back without arguing.
Andrew caught Darius's eye across the table. Darius shook his head, but the corner of his mouth moved.

They cleared the food. Yelena produced her cards again. Nico challenged Mara to a game whose rules he began revising before she had agreed to play. Sera wanted to know whether anyone had fixed the projector. Akari said they could always watch Juno explain the bearing again, and Juno offered to draw diagrams.
Andrew laughed with the others, then glanced through the door.
Mara had left the patrol sheet on his desk. He could see it from here. Ten minutes would finish it. There was still the morning briefing to prepare and a simulator run he'd promised himself.
He stood and began gathering plates.
Juno reached for the stack. “I've got those.”
“There's a lot.”
“I've noticed.”
Andrew let him take them.
Across the room, Sera slid a scrap of paper beneath the projector's rear foot. The picture on the far wall tilted, steadied, and resolved into a menu.
“Fixed,” she said.
Juno turned with the plates still in his hands. “It needed a replacement mount.”
Sera tapped the folded paper.
“That's a temporary solution,” he said.
“So is the film. It's ninety minutes.”

Andrew stayed to hear which film they were arguing about. Then he stayed long enough to take Yelena's side, which turned out to be a mistake because she changed her vote as soon as Darius disagreed with her.
By the time he slipped out, Nico was trying to trade a week of somebody else's chores for the right to choose.
The corridor was cool after the crowded room. Andrew rubbed the back of his neck, sat at his desk and unfolded Mara's sheet.
She had marked the flooded approach and drawn the service road in a firm, clean line. Beside it she'd added the turning space they'd need if they had to bring a mech back under tow.
He worked through the new route. At the bottom of the page he put a question beside Juno's inspection, ready for the morning, and checked the departure time against the forecast.
The film started next door. Someone complained about the volume. Somebody else made it louder.
Andrew reached for his coffee, remembered it, and left the mug alone.

A photograph was pinned beside the desk lamp. Twelve of them stood between two mechs, crowded close because Akari had insisted everyone fit. Matthias had hooked two fingers through the back of Andrew's collar just as the picture was taken. Andrew was laughing and trying to pull away. He couldn't remember what had been said.
He straightened the corner that had curled away from the wall, then returned to the page.
Bootsteps stopped outside his door.
Darius stood there with a plate and a little jar.
“You missed this,” he said.
“I ate.”
“I know. I watched you.”
On the plate sat the half roll Darius had saved from his dinner, split and toasted. He unscrewed the jar and spread a thin layer of jam across it, working carefully to reach the edges.
Andrew looked at the label. Strawberry. He hadn't seen strawberry jam in weeks.
“Where'd you get that?”
“I have arrangements.”
“With who?”
“People who appreciate bread.”
Darius set the plate in the one space Andrew hadn't covered with paper. He noticed the photograph, glanced at it, then rested his hip against the desk.
“Good dinner,” Andrew said.
“Wasn't what I planned.”
“Still good.”
Darius watched him take a bite. The bread cracked under his teeth, and the jam was sweet enough to make him close his eyes for a moment.
“You should come back,” Darius said.
Andrew swallowed. “I've got the briefing.”
Darius looked down at the sheet. Andrew had written BRIEFING across the top and underlined it twice.
“Looks brief.”
“That's a terrible joke.”
“You usually like those.”
Andrew smiled despite himself. He moved the plate to see the last section of the map.
Darius stayed where he was.
“What?” Andrew asked.
“Nothing.”
From the common room came a burst of laughter. Andrew recognized Mara's, loud and surprised. It made him look toward the door.
He had checked the route. Mara had checked it. Juno would give him the inspection results in the morning. There was nothing on the page that needed another ten minutes tonight.
He laid the pencil across the map.
“If Nico picked the film, I'm blaming you.”
Darius pushed away from the desk. “Fair.”
Andrew took his plate with him.
There was a space on the couch beside Akari. She lifted her feet to let him through, then put them straight back across his knees once he sat down.
“I charge for this,” Andrew told her.
“Put it on my account.”

On the wall, a man in an immaculate suit was trying to climb through a kitchen window. Nico insisted they had missed the best part. Sera told him the best part had been hearing the film before he started talking again.
Andrew settled back. He'd take ten minutes.
Then Akari reached for his toast.
He caught her wrist without looking away from the screen.
“Ask Darius.”
“I did. He said you'd share.”
Andrew looked across the room. Darius was opening the jam jar for Juno, who had finally finished the dishes. He caught Andrew's expression and gave him a small, unrepentant shrug.
Andrew broke the toast in half.
